why: Express the CommonJS way. Every handler shape: a bare local function, `exports.version` in the same module, `users.list` through a `require` namespace (the route-separation idiom), an inline arrow, a router mounted with `app.use`. Two router bindings: the direct `const app = express()` and the chained `var app = module.exports = express()` that 18 of express's 28 example apps use. Plus a computed path, and a renamed export — `exports.destroy = helper` beside a private `function destroy` — whose route must bind to `helper`. (An earlier version routed to `users.missing`, an export that does not exist; Express throws on an undefined handler at start-up, so that Endpoint could never have existed, and the fixture was stating something false. The dropped-EXPOSES rule is pinned by a unit test instead.)

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `users.destroy` is what `users.js` exports as `destroy`, which is `helper`. A private `function destroy` exists beside it; resolving the handler by id alone bound the route to it. The export map routes it to `helper`.

excluded: `GET /inline` has an Endpoint and no EXPOSES by design: an inline arrow is no named symbol, and inventing a handler id would be the fabrication the route reader refuses.
`/computed/${1}` yields no Endpoint: a template literal is refused even with a constant substitution, because a wrong path would be presented as grounded.
`res.send(...)` — member calls on an untyped parameter.
`express()` / `express.Router()` are top-level calls, outside any function body, so no caller exists to hang a CALLS edge on.
